Pigeon Checkers

InvariantsParity

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: jump counters from the left half of the board to the right. Jumped counters stay — they are not taken off.
How to play: click a counter, then an empty cell two steps away (straight or diagonal). Try the Hint shading if you get stuck.
Look for the math

The board is N rows by N+1 columns. Counters start in a triangle on the left. Every jump preserves the parity of a counter's coordinates — so some shaded cells can never receive a counter that did not begin on that shade. That is a pigeonhole argument: too many counters want seats that the right half does not have.

What a jump keeps fixed

A legal jump moves by (±2, 0), (0, ±2) or (±2, ±2). In every case both x mod 2 and y mod 2 stay the same, so a counter on an even–even cell (the Hint's filled dots) never leaves that lattice. The jumped counter is not removed — only the jumper moves.

Odd N and even N

For every N from 2 to 20, the starting triangle puts a different number of even–even counters on the left half than the right half can hold. The logic test checks that mismatch, and exhaustively searches N = 2 and N = 3 to confirm the right half is unreachable. The page's odd-N diagram and even-N checkerboard colouring are two ways of seeing the same obstruction.

Removing a few does not help

The page notes that taking one or two counters off the left at the start still leaves the colouring unbalanced. The invariant cares about how many counters sit on each shade, not only the total count.

Turn on Hint and watch which counters can never cross the midline.
